header.title_plain: Eight weeks of maximal jumping made every muscle fibre type bigger, stronger and faster — including slow-twitch
header.setup_plain: Eight recreationally active men did eight weeks of maximal bodyweight jumping — static, countermovement, drop, triple and hurdle jumps, 24 sessions, 5,228 jumps in all. Individual muscle fibres from the thigh were tested for size, force, speed and power before and after. No control group.

citation.title: Stretch-shortening cycle exercises: an effective training paradigm to enhance power output of human single muscle fibers
citation.authors: Malisoux L, Francaux M, Nielens H, Theisen D

header.evidence_type: Pre/post intervention, single group, no control, 8 men. Lab single-fibre measurements plus functional tests.

confidence.why: Clean mechanistic data, but tiny, uncontrolled and all young men.

practical_relevance.why: Gives a specific bodyweight plyometric protocol (3×/week for 8 weeks) with jump, leg-press and shuttle gains, and shows a fibre-velocity effect conventional lifting has not shown.

header.funding_and_conflicts: Funded by a university research fund.

groups.name: Plyometric (SSC)
groups.protocol: Bodyweight jumps, max effort, progressive: static & countermovement jumps, 40-cm drop jumps, double/single-leg triple jumps, hurdle jumps. Sessions 20 → ~45 min
groups.training_status: recreationally active ~3 h/wk; no prior jump training

intervention.design_notes: No control group. Duration: 8 weeks. Compliance 100%. Biopsies from vastus lateralis 3 days after each test session; 1,115 fibres pre, 1,002 post typed; 60–80 per fibre type tested mechanically. Single-fibre measurements on skinned (dissected, chemically treated) fibres at 15 °C. Comparison the authors draw: 12 weeks of conventional resistance training (Widrick 2002) raised type I and IIa fibre power 30% and 42% through size and force alone, with no change in shortening velocity.

measured.outcome: Force per area (specific tension) — all fibre types
Power per volume — types I, IIa/IIx

layer2.what_it_means: Jump training did more than make these men jump higher. At the level of individual muscle fibres it increased size, force, contraction speed and power across the board — and, unusually, it sped up slow-twitch fibres as well as fast ones. Conventional lifting in comparable studies grows fibres and makes them stronger but doesn't make them faster. So plyometrics appear to train a quality (shortening velocity) that heavy lifting doesn't, and the whole-body results followed: +13% countermovement jump, +12% leg press, faster shuttle run. Three bodyweight sessions a week were enough.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: Eight young, already-active men and no control group: any change over eight weeks of being in a study is attributed to the jumps. The single-fibre measurements are made on dissected, chemically treated fibres at 15 °C — a window into mechanism, not a performance test. The fibre-type shifts didn't reach significance. The authors are explicit that they can't prove the fast contractions caused the faster fibres. Nothing here about women, older adults, or combining plyometrics with lifting, and 5,228 maximal jumps in 8 weeks is a substantial load that was progressed carefully and supervised.

translation: Protocol: bodyweight jumps at max effort, 3×/week for 8 weeks, ~20 rising to ~45 min, drop jumps from 40 cm, hurdle and single-leg variants added as tolerated, ~220 jumps per session on average.
Result: vertical jump +9–13%, leg press +12%, 5-m shuttle −4%.
Distinctive effect: fibres got faster, not just bigger — something lifting alone hasn't shown.

glossary_candidates.definition: A fast lengthening of a muscle immediately followed by a powerful shortening — the mechanism of jumping, bounding, and plyometrics.
Jump-based training that exploits the stretch-shortening cycle.
A vertical jump with a quick dip first; the standard test of lower-body power.
The thickness of a muscle or fibre; the main driver of how much force it can produce.
Force divided by fibre size; unchanged here, meaning fibres got stronger by getting bigger, not by improving quality.
How fast a fibre contracts with no load; faster fibres make more power.
Fibres containing more than one myosin type (e.g. IIa/IIx); common and intermediate in properties.
A single muscle fibre with its membrane removed so it can be activated and measured in a dish.
